argument_macro_structure.dominant_argument_form: Modus tollens and reductio ad absurdum
argument_macro_structure.premise_explicitness: Mixed: some premises are explicit, others are implicit and reconstructed from Hick's texts

argumentative_quality.dialectical_reasonableness: High: engages with Hick's later defense and anticipates objections
argumentative_quality.logical_relevance: High: all premises directly support the thesis
argumentative_quality.premise_acceptability: Moderate: relies on anthropological evidence and internal consistency of Hick's views

distinctions_drawn: The Real as ineffable vs. experienced
explicit_definitions_given: Religious experience as 'modifications in the content of consciousness' employing religious concepts
Soteriological effectiveness as criterion for truthfulness

dialectical_engagement.objection_handling: Anticipates and responds to Hick's ethical criterion defense, showing it fails to exclude pre-axial religions
objections_raised: Hick might claim pre-axial religions are delusory
Hick's later defense using ethical criterion
Hick's selection of post-axial religions as providing the right criterion

appeals_to_authority: Ward and Mavrodes for philosophical context
method_and_evidence.evidence_type: Empirical examples from indigenous religions, textual analysis of Hick's works

philosophical_orientation.sentiment: Critical but constructive; aims to improve pluralistic hypothesis
philosophical_orientation.thematic_focus: Religious diversity, pluralism, exclusivism, religious experience

structural_organization.structure_type: Problem-solution with internal critique and objection-reply

summary_of_core_decisions: The article's core decision is to apply Hick's own parity-of-experience principle to pre-axial religions, exposing an arbitrary exclusion. It then critiques the soteriological criterion as unjustified, and finally argues that any adequate pluralism must include all religious experience.

thesis_commitment.hedging_density_in_final_paragraph: Low: states conclusion firmly but acknowledges broader oversight
